abstract: Astronomers spot an unprecedented double disk of debris around a dead star.
title: First-of-its-kind planetary wreckage holds clues to our Solar System’s fate

abstract: Abstract RNA language models have achieved strong performances across diverse downstream tasks by leveraging large-scale sequence data. However, RNA function is fundamentally shaped by its hierarchical structure, making the integration of structural information into pre-training essential. Existing methods often depend on noisy structural annotations or introduce task-specific biases, limiting model generalizability. Here, we introduce structRFM, a structure-guided RNA foundation model that is pre-trained on millions of RNA sequences and secondary structures data by integrating base pairing interactions into masked language modeling through a novel pair matching operation. The structure-guided mask and nucleotide-level mask are further balanced by a dynamic masking ratio. structRFM learns joint knowledge of sequential and structural data, producing versatile representations, including classification-level, sequence-level, and pairwise matrix features, that support a broad spectrum of downstream adaptations. structRFM ranks among the top models in zero-shot homology classification across fifteen biological language models, and sets new benchmarks for secondary structure prediction. structRFM further derives Zfold, which enables robust and reliable tertiary structure prediction, with consistent improvements in estimating 3D structures and their accordingly extracted 2D structures, achieving a pronounced 19% performance gain compared with AlphaFold3 on RNA Puzzles dataset. In functional tasks such as internal ribosome entry site identification, structRFM achieves a whopping 49% performance gain in F1 score. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of structure-guided pre-training and highlight a promising direction for developing multi-modal RNA language models in computational biology. To support the broader scientific community, we have made the 21-million sequence-structure dataset and the pre-trained structRFM model fully open-source, facilitating the development of multimodal foundation models in biology.
title: An open structure-guided RNA foundation model for generalizable prediction

abstract: BACKGROUND: messenger RNA, lowers triglyceride levels and potentially mitigates the risk of acute pancreatitis. METHODS: In two double-blind, placebo-controlled trials, 757 adults with severe hypertriglyceridemia were randomly assigned in a 2:1 ratio to receive plozasiran (25 mg) or placebo at baseline and at months 3, 6, and 9. These trials had identical designs, end points, and analytic plans. The primary end point was the percent change in the fasting plasma triglyceride level from baseline to month 12. Key secondary end points were the percent change in the fasting triglyceride level from baseline to month 10, a fasting triglyceride level of less than 500 mg per deciliter (5.6 mmol per liter) and less than 150 mg per deciliter (1.7 mmol per liter), the percent change in the fasting serum triglyceride level at month 12 for patients with a baseline triglyceride level of 880 mg per deciliter or greater, and changes in remnant cholesterol and non-HDL cholesterol. A pooled analysis addressed adjudicated acute pancreatitis, incidence, and first-event timing. RESULTS: At month 12, patients in the plozasiran groups had a median triglyceride level that was lower than the baseline level by 79% and 81% in the two trials. These reductions corresponded to a median difference in the plozasiran groups as compared with the placebo groups (placebo-adjusted change) of -45 percentage points (95% confidence interval [CI], -51 to -38) and -47 percentage points (95% CI, -54 to -39). A triglyceride level of less than 500 mg per deciliter at 12 months was reported in 91% and 93% of the patients in the plozasiran groups and in 51% and 50% of those in the placebo groups (P<0.001). The rates of acute pancreatitis were 1 per 100 patient-years with plozasiran and 5 per 100 patient-years with placebo (rate ratio, 0.22; P = 0.008). Adverse events during treatment occurred in 73% of the patients in both the pooled plozasiran and placebo groups. CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with severe hypertriglyceridemia, the use of plozasiran resulted in lower triglyceride levels and a lower risk of acute pancreatitis than placebo at 12 months. (Funded by Arrowhead Pharmaceuticals; SHASTA-3 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06347003; SHASTA-4, NCT06347016.).
title: Plozasiran for Severe Hypertriglyceridemia and Risk of Pancreatitis

abstract: Pioneering thermal transport measurements on two-dimensional electron gases in high magnetic fields have demonstrated that the quantized Hall state at filling factor ν = 5/2 has a thermal Hall conductance κ quantized in half-integer multiples of κ 0 = π 2 k B 2 T / 3 h . Half-integer κ / κ 0 is a signature of neutral Majorana edge modes, in turn linked to the presence of non-Abelian anyon excitations in the bulk. However, the experimentally observed value of κ corresponds to the “PH-Pfaffian” state, in tension with numerical studies which instead favor either the Pfaffian or the AntiPfaffian. A variety of mechanisms have been invoked to explain this discrepancy, but have been either ruled out by further experiments or else involve fine-tuning. Building on density-matrix-renormalization group studies of physically realistic edges and analytic calculations of edge structure, we propose an alternative resolution of this puzzle involving an “edge reconstruction” solely involving the neutral Majorana sector of the theory. Such a Majorana edge reconstruction can “screen” a Pfaffian or AntiPfaffian bulk, so that transport signatures become indistinguishable from those of the PH-Pfaffian. We argue that this physically natural scenario is consistent with experiment.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Majorana edge reconstruction and the ν = 5/2 non-Abelian thermal Hall puzzle

abstract: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a severe autoimmune connective tissue disease characterized by immune dysregulation and progressive fibrosis of the skin and internal organs, resulting in substantial organ dysfunction and increased mortality. Fibrosis is driven in part by infiltration of immune cells, including monocytes that become activated within fibrotic tissue. However, how the mechanical properties of fibrotic skin regulate their function remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that increased stiffness activates human monocytes through mechanosensing. Reanalysis of single cell RNA sequencing datasets revealed that skin infiltrating monocytes exhibit heightened inflammatory signatures as compared to circulating counterparts, with further amplification in SSc. Using collagen-coated hydrogels modeling physiological and fibrotic stiffness, we show that increased stiffness enhances CD86 expression, and broadly upregulates inflammatory transcriptional programs in human monocytes. Mechanistically, stiffness-driven activation was associated with chromatin remodeling and epigenetic reprogramming, identifying the transcription factor Specificity Protein 1 (SP1) as a central regulator. CRISPR–Cas9-mediated disruption or pharmacologic inhibition of SP1 significantly attenuated stiffness- induced inflammatory gene expression, whereas we found no evidence for involvement of the canonical YAP/TAZ–TEAD axis, and pharmacological modulation of PIEZO1 neither reproduced nor blocked the response. Further, monocytes from patients with SSc displayed altered transcriptional trajectories and an exaggerated inflammatory response to high stiffness, accompanied by reduced expression of wound healing and antifibrotic programs. Together, these findings identify SP1-dependent mechanosensing as a previously unrecognized pathway controlling human monocyte activation in the skin and provide mechanistic insight into how tissue stiffness sustains inflammation in SSc.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Dysregulation of mechanosensing signaling in monocytes of patients with systemic sclerosis is associated with skin inflammation

abstract: Halide perovskites have emerged as promising materials for next-generation photovoltaics, laser sources, and X-ray detectors. There is intense debate as to whether some photoactive halide perovskites exhibit ferroelectric behavior and whether it might be possible to utilize the bulk photovoltaic effect to enhance the performance of halide perovskite solar cells. Here, using low-dose scanning transmission electron microscopy, we identify ferroelastic twin walls in vapor-deposited CsPbI 3 thin films, parallel to {110} and {112}. Remarkably, despite CsPbI 3 being centrosymmetric and nonpolar, we observe directly that Pb atoms shift at {110} twin walls driving a local ferroelectric-like polarization. These polar twin walls form an intrinsic array of nanoscale interfaces, spaced ~30 to 50 nm apart, embedded within the nonpolar perovskite lattice. In contrast, {112} twin walls do not show a polar displacement of Pb but strongly suppress octahedral tilt and off-center Cs atom displacements, revealing a different untapped structural degree of freedom. These findings reveal previously hidden nanoscale polarization in halide perovskite semiconductors, opening opportunities for enhanced conductivity and photovoltaic behavior through domain wall engineering.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Polarized twin walls in a halide perovskite

abstract: Gas mixing in porous media governs important environmental and industrial applications in which multiple gas components share the available pore space with liquid water, simultaneously undergoing gas mixing and gas–liquid redistribution. Currently, this process is represented by macroscopic models that ignore pore scale dynamics. We demonstrate that this is not generally valid, and can lead to large errors in the mixing rate. We use 4D X-ray imaging to investigate nitrogen injection into a porous sandstone saturated with krypton and water, jointly imaging the gas mixture composition evolution and multiphase flow of gas and water. In contrast to the smooth, continuous representation of the conventional advection–diffusion model, our results show that gas mixing evolves through a sequence of distinct regimes controlled by gas connectivity. Initially, immiscible gas–water displacement generates gas composition variance as the different gases occupy neighboring pores separated by water. As gas connectivity increases, intermittent gas–liquid interfacial rearrangements rapidly connect regions of contrasting gas composition, driving a fast decay in composition variance. Once connectivity stabilizes, mixing is controlled by a confined diffusion process within the quasi-static gas network. At later times, further mixing is driven slowly by multicomponent Ostwald ripening, whereby trapped gas ganglia exchange solutes through the surrounding liquid phase. These findings provide insights into gas mixing in porous media, suggesting concepts for upscaling the role of pore scale multiphase flow in gas mixing in the subsurface.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Intermittent gas–liquid rearrangement controls the mixing of gases in porous media

abstract: t-distributed Stochastic Neighborhood Embedding (t-SNE) has gained popularity as a dimension reduction technique, especially for visualizing data. It is well-known that dimension reduction may lose important data features. We provide a mathematical framework for understanding this loss for t-SNE, establishing several quantitative results across different scenarios that demonstrate how important structural information is lost.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Some theoretical limitations of t-SNE

abstract: Plants synthesize diverse phenylpropanoids, which provide us essential medicine, nutrients, and biomaterials while also acting as a major global carbon sink. Phenylpropanoids are primarily derived from L-phenylalanine (Phe) via Phe ammonia-lyase (PAL), a highly regulated enzymatic activity that limits phenylpropanoid production. However, it remains poorly understood how different plant species regulate PAL enzymes. Phylogeny-guided biochemical screening uncovered complex and diverse feedback regulation of PAL enzymes from 14 different plant species. This screening found a previously uncharacterized PAL clade, namely PALnc (from noncanonical), with some members exhibiting feedback activation by p -coumaric acid, caffeic acid, and 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvic acid in vitro. Transient expression of two PALnc genes, from Elaeis guineensis ( EgPALnc ) and Piper methysticum ( PmPALnc2 ), in Nicotiana benthamiana leaves elevated phenylpropanoid content, supported by the high in planta stability of PALnc proteins compared to canonical PALs. Whereas overexpression of Arabidopsis thaliana PAL1 ( AtPAL1 ) in stable Arabidopsis transgenic lines resulted in very low accumulation of AtPAL1 protein and minor metabolic effects, introduction of EgPALnc rendered high content of EgPALnc protein and hyperaccumulation of hydroxycinnamates derivatives. Our findings uncover a previously overlooked diversity in the regulation of the entry step of phenylpropanoid biosynthesis across various plants and identify atypical PALs within the PALnc clade as valuable tools to debottleneck and enhance phenylpropanoid production in planta.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Atypical phenylalanine ammonia-lyases that enhance phenylpropanoid production in plants

abstract: Abstract Compartmental models of infectious disease transmission make assumptions about human behaviors. Specifically, they parameterize interactions across population groups, assumed to have distinct epidemiologically-relevant behavioral patterns, primarily through contact matrices stratified by demographic variables such as age, gender, or socioeconomic status. Although such demographic characteristics are readily measurable, they may inadequately capture the social and psychological forces that govern protective behaviors. Drawing on 20 waves of a national survey conducted throughout the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States, we show that institutional trust — particularly trust in public health agencies, physicians, and hospitals — is a dominant predictor of protective behavior adoption. For mask wearing during periods of strongest pandemic activity, for example, institutional trust explains more behavioral variance across population groups than age, income, education, and partisan affiliation combined. In unadjusted analyses, the difference in protective behavior adoption between individuals with the highest and lowest trust in the CDC was four- to six-fold larger than the corresponding differences by age, income, or educational attainment, and exceeded the difference between Democratic and Republican respondents. This association was institutionally specific (e.g., the relationship attenuates for trust in banks), and behaviorally specific (e.g., trust in the CDC is associated with protective behaviors but not visiting a doctor). The latter suggests that trust modifies voluntary compliance with public health recommendations rather than access to or use of healthcare. We conclude that compartmental models of disease transmission would be substantially improved by incorporating institutional trust as a stratifying variable. We additionally offer a trust-integrated mathematical modeling framework and recommendations for the data infrastructure needed for its implementation.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Trust as a hidden driver of epidemic-relevant behavior: Institution- and behavior-specific associations across 20 national survey waves

abstract: Abstract Existing research has found that shared neural responses to naturalistic narratives are associated with shared understanding, especially among members of the same social group. In this fMRI study, we tested whether in-group neural synchronization solely reflects explicit shared understandings, or relates to other group characteristics. To do so, we compared the neural synchronization patterns among two distinct social groups: Religious ( N = 21) and Secular ( N = 21). Participants were scanned while watching short video clips containing religious or neutral content and then answered questions regarding their reactions to- and interpretation of the videos. Behavioral results did not reveal group differences in responses’ homogeneity: neither in the engagement and agreement while watching the videos, nor in the emotions and verbal reactions elicited by it. However, neuroimaging results revealed that religious participants exhibited strikingly higher in-group synchronization than secular, both for religious and neutral narratives. Remarkably, it was possible to predict individuals’ religious affiliation solely based on their in-group neural synchrony, with accuracy scores of up to 92%. This pattern was consistent across all neural networks, most prominently in the Default Mode Network (DMN), Control and Attention networks. It also emerged in the Salience network and Somatomotor regions, hinting at neural processes that may foster group cohesion and identification. We propose that increased neural synchrony in the Religious group was driven mainly by greater homogenous social structure, suggesting a novel perspective for interpreting the role of neural synchrony in group dynamics.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: In-group neural alignment serves as a biomarker of social identity

abstract: Abstract Conventional histological relies on fixation, embedding, sectioning, and staining methods that distort cellular architecture, extract lipids, and introduces variability, limiting reproducibility. We present Normalized Stimulated Raman Imaging (NoRI) that enables quantitative, label-free protein and lipid measurements at high-spatial resolution. NoRI computationally corrects protein, lipid, and water Raman signals, allowing quantitative biomass measurements while preserving tissue architecture, facilitating analysis by convolutional neural networks. Applied to mouse kidney, NoRI accurately classified tubule types (F1-[harmonic mean of precision and recall against manual annotation]=0.93), anatomical regions (F1=0.91), and biological sex (F1=0.97), revealing greater cytoplasmic lipid (+6.9mg/mL; p=0.028) and nuclear protein (+26.3mg/mL; p<0.001) in female tubules. In acute kidney injury, NoRI captured dynamic lipid and protein organization and quantified brush border remodelling and lipid droplet changes over 25 days. Spatial lipid quantification was central for feature classification in AKI (F1=1.0). These results establish NoRI as a reproducible, quantitative method for diagnostics, histopathology, and feature discovery.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Normalized Raman imaging for studies of tissue physiology of the kidney

abstract: We measure the spatial pattern associated with the superradiant emission from a cloud of cold 87Rb atoms using Fourier imaging. We observe a highly directional, ring-shaped emission structure, which corresponds to a single collective jump operator associated to the most superradiant mode of the ensemble. Using spatial filtering, we isolate this channel and find the typical superradiant burst with superlinear scaling of the intensity with atom number. We compare our results to two models that describe the competition between the various decay channels, finding good agreement. Our work shows that the collective jump operators introduced by Carmichael et al. [Optics Communications 179, 417 (2000)] can be measured and manipulated.
title: Fourier imaging of collective spontaneous emission modes in superradiant cold atomic clouds

abstract: We argue that the low-temperature physics of $S=1$ pyrochlore magnets with a predominantly Ising-like easy-axis exchange coupling $J$ that favors the local tetrahedral body diagonals, and a comparably large easy-plane single-ion anisotropy $Δ=J + μ$ ($|μ| \ll J$) that favors the plane perpendicular to these local axes will exhibit interesting new phenomena due to the competition between $J$ and $Δ$. In the $T/J \rightarrow 0$ limit, we find three low temperature phases as a function of $μ/T$: a short-range correlated paramagnetic phase, and two topologically-distinct Coulomb liquids separated by a $Z_2$ flux confinement transition. Both Coulomb liquids are described at long-wavelengths by a fluctuating divergence-free polarization field and have characteristic pinch-point singularities in their structure factor. In one Coulomb phase, the flux of this polarization field is confined to {\em even} integers, while it takes on all integer values in the other Coulomb phase. Experimental realizations with $|μ| \ll J$ and negative are predicted to exhibit signatures of a transition from a flux-deconfined Coulomb phase to the flux-confined Coulomb phase as they are cooled below $T_{c_2} \approx 1.57|μ|$, while realizations with positive $μ\ll J$ will show signatures of a transition from a flux-deconfined Coulomb liquid to a short-range correlated paramagnet via a continuous $XY$-like transition at $T_{c_1} \approx 0.98 μ$.
title: S = 1 pyrochlore magnets with competing anisotropies: A tale of two Coulomb phases, Z 2 flux confinement, and XY-like transitions

abstract: Single electron spins can be used to encode and process information in semiconductor quantum devices. Progress has been hindered by materials challenges, such as the small energy splitting between low-lying valley states and hyperfine coupling to nuclear spins. Here we use density functional theory to optimize the valley splitting and spin dephasing time in realistic Si/SiGe heterostructures. Reductions in the Si quantum well width generally increase the valley splitting. However, in narrow quantum wells, a larger fraction of the electronic wavefunction resides in the SiGe buffer layers, which increases the hyperfine coupling with spinful $^{73}$Ge. Our work shows that Si/SiGe heterostructures with 3~--~4~nm wide quantum wells and $^{73}$Ge and $^{29}$Si concentrations of 50 ppm should support average valley splittings $E_{v}$~$>$~500~$μ$eV and spin dephasing times $T_2^*$ exceeding 15~$μ$s assuming an effective quantum dot area of 700 nm$^2$. In addition, sharper Si/SiGe interfaces in general result in larger valley splittings and longer spin dephasing times.
title: Co-optimization of spin coherence and valley splitting in Si/SiGe heterostructures

abstract: We search for possible charmonium(-like) states decaying into the $p\bar{p}$ final state by studying the Born cross sections of the $e^+e^-\to p\bar{p}$ reaction, and we determine the proton electromagnetic form factors by analyzing the proton angular distribution. The measurement is performed using a sample of $e^+e^-$ collision data collected at 47 center-of-mass energies from 3.510 to 4.946 GeV, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 26 fb$^{-1}$, recorded by the BESIII detector collected at the BEPCII collider. The decay $ψ(3770)\to p\bar{p}$ is observed with a significance of 6.6$σ$ including systematic uncertainties. Furthermore, a structure near 4.2 GeV is observed with significances of $4.6σ$ or $4.8σ$ for the $ψ(4160)$ or $Y(4230)$ hypotheses including systematic uncertainties, respectively; these interpretations cannot presently be distinguished. In addition, the moduli of the form factor ratios $|G_{E}/G_{M}|$ and of the magnetic form factors $|G_{M}|$ are extracted by analyzing the proton polar angle distribution with higher precision at large time-like squared momentum transfer. These results provide important experimental insights into both the decay mechanisms of charmonium(-like) states in the open charm region and the internal structure of proton.
title: Observation of ψ ( 3770 ) → p p ‾ and measurement of electromagnetic form factors of proton at s = 3.510 − 4.946 GeV

abstract: Inclusive hadronic decay widths remain a long-standing challenge for first-principles QCD. We present a framework combining lattice QCD with strongly-coupled potential nonrelativistic QCD (pNRQCD) to compute inclusive P-wave heavy quarkonium decays to light hadrons. At leading order in the velocity expansion, all nonperturbative effects, apart from the square of the derivative of the wavefunction at the origin, are encoded in a single universal moment of the two-point chromoelectric correlator, which we determine for the first time from a quenched lattice QCD calculation matched to $\overline{\mathrm{MS}}$ via the gradient flow. Combined with perturbative short-distance coefficients and the square of the derivative of the wavefunction at the origin, our result reproduces the observed $χ_{cJ}(1P)$ widths and, at the same time, provides predictions for the unmeasured $χ_{bJ}(nP)$ widths. The framework extends naturally to inclusive decays and production of ordinary and exotic hadrons.
title: Inclusive P -wave quarkonium decay widths from lattice QCD and potential nonrelativistic QCD

abstract: The pseudogap stands out in the phase diagram of the cuprate high-temperature superconductors because its origin and relationship to superconductivity remain elusive. The origin of the pseudogap has been debated, with competing hypotheses attributing it to preformed electron pairs or local order, such as charge density waves. We present unambiguous evidence supporting the pairing scenario, using local shot-noise spectroscopy measurements in Bi 2 Sr 2 CaCu 2 O 8+δ . Our data demonstrate that the pseudogap energy coincides with the onset of electron pairing and is spatially heterogeneous with values reaching up to 70 milli–electron volts. Our results exclude a pure local order origin of the pseudogap, link the pseudogap to Cooper pair formation, and suggest that the limiting factor for higher critical temperature in cuprates is phase coherence.
title: Equivalence of pseudogap and pairing energy in a cuprate high-temperature superconductor

abstract: Molecules that modulate protein-protein interactions, including through ternary complex formation, have been established as key therapeutics. Yet they can be challenging to discover, as standard screening approaches often lack throughput or fail to directly assay multibody interactions. We addressed this by combining DNA nanoswitch–based selection of nucleotide-encoded libraries with next-generation sequencing to create FIND (Functional Interaction–based Nanoswitch Discovery), which enables ultrahigh-throughput discovery of compounds that induce or increase protein-protein interactions. We demonstrate FIND by discovering nanobodies that stabilize the interaction between angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 and the receptor-binding domain of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 and by discovering agonists of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor gamma from a DNA-barcoded small-molecule library. By enabling rapid discovery of molecular modulators, FIND could lead to new therapeutics across many conditions.
title: Discovering molecular modulators with nanoswitch screening

abstract: Anthropogenic noise is a rapidly expanding global pollutant, but its effects across biological levels from individuals to ecosystems remain unquantified. We conducted phylogenetically controlled meta-analyses of 214 experimental studies on 177 aquatic and terrestrial species with ranges that span six continents. Noise altered at least one physiological, developmental, or behavioral trait in 80% of species studied, with declines in fitness and abundance and disruptions of predator-prey interactions. Effects occurred in every habitat, although response mechanisms varied for some traits and species, creating winners and losers. Only multispecies analyses can reveal such species- and ecosystem-level impacts of anthropogenic stressors. Our results establish noise as a novel selection pressure reshaping ecosystem dynamics and as a pervasive stressor requiring soundscape protection alongside habitat conservation.
title: Echoes of the Anthropocene: Noise pollution as a global threat

abstract: Cancer-associated hematopoietic abnormalities contribute to systemic immunosuppression. However, whether tumors can initiate localized extramedullary hematopoiesis to suppress antitumor immunity remains unclear. In this study, we identify a distinct form of hepatic hematopoiesis driven by liver metastasis–associated hematopoietic stem cells (LM-HSCs). Liver metastases establish ectopic periportal hematopoietic niches that recruit bone marrow HSCs through Kupffer cell–dependent C-C motif chemokine receptor 1 (CCR1) signaling. Although LM-HSCs retain self-renewal and multipotency, cAMP response element–binding protein (CREB) activation skews their differentiation toward the myeloid lineage, particularly annexin A1–positive (ANXA1 + ) immature neutrophils. These neutrophils produce glucocorticoids, which activate glucocorticoid receptor signaling in a paracrine manner and induce immune checkpoint receptor expression and functional anergy in CD8 + T and natural killer cells. Collectively, these findings suggest that liver metastases reprograms hepatic hematopoiesis to promote immunosuppression.
title: Tumor metastasis co-opts liver hematopoiesis to promote immunosuppression

abstract: Ultracold atom platforms enable low temperatures and long free evolution times, which are crucial for fundamental physics tests and atom interferometry. The lowest equivalent temperature reported in such a system is 38 pK with a free expansion time of 2 s, achieved in atom-chip-based magnetic traps in microgravity. Optical dipole trap (ODT) systems offer better optical access and the flexibility to condense both magnetic and non-magnetic atoms, but have not been used to prepare quantum degenerate gases under microgravity conditions. Here we report an ODT-based Bose-Einstein condensate created aboard the China Space Station, containing 2.0 × 10 4 atoms, reaching an equivalent temperature of 9.7 − 2.7 + 3.2 pK with a free expansion time of 7.0 s. This record-low temperature could stimulate a new generation of ODT-based experiments in quantum simulation and precision measurements in space.
title: Quantum gases below 10 picokelvin in space

abstract: Dansgaard-Oeschger (DO) events during the last ice age are thought to reflect rapid shifts in the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC). Greenland ice cores suggest warming transitions within only a few decades—or even just over 10 years. Using precisely dated speleothem oxygen-isotope records from the Asian monsoon region, we have shown that the same DO warmings unfolded over more than a century. Isotope modeling revealed that Greenland records primarily capture a rapid atmospheric reorganization triggered by the initial sea-ice retreat in the northeastern North Atlantic, whereas the parallel AMOC recovery and hemispheric thermal adjustment proceeded much more slowly. These findings reveal that natural AMOC transitions evolved more slowly than the rapid North Greenland oxygen-isotope shifts would imply, thereby refining our understanding of “abruptness” during DO events.
title: Glacial abrupt transitions in ocean circulation were much slower than ice-core records imply

abstract: Excessive androgens serve as a primary driver for many phenotypic features of polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS). Although dietary fiber has been shown to alleviate PMOS, its effects on androgen concentrations and the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. In a clinical trial, we demonstrated that a dietary fiber combination consisting of inulin, resistant starch, and β-glucan reduces androgen concentrations in patients’ plasma. Mechanistically, dietary fiber increased the abundance of Bacteroides xylanisolven s, which converts androstenedione into a nonandrogenic secondary hormone metabolite we named coproandrosterone, which is further metabolized by gut microbiota into dihydro-coproandrosterone. This metabolic pathway was validated in a mouse model. These findings highlight the potential of dietary fiber to alleviate PMOS by modulating androgen homeostasis through gut microbiota, offering insights for prebiotic and probiotic therapies.
title: Targeting hormone conversion through dietary fiber improves polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome

abstract: Adipose tissue undergoes extensive remodeling to adapt to changing physiological demands. This plasticity encompasses changes in adipocyte metabolism and number, extracellular matrix organization, vascularization, immune composition, and innervation. When coordinated, these processes preserve energy buffering, thermogenesis, endocrine function, and local tissue support. Pathological adipose tissue remodeling drives obesity-related complications and contributes to many diseases involving organ-associated adipose depots throughout the body. In cancer, tumor-associated fat can develop a metabolic and fibroinflammatory niche that promotes tumor growth and invasion, and remodeling of other depots can directly disrupt neighboring tissues. Recent studies have identified mesenchymal, immune, vascular, and adipocyte states that govern adaptive or pathological outcomes. These findings broaden therapeutic goals beyond reducing fat mass toward restoring adipogenesis, substrate turnover, thermogenic capacity, and tissue-niche function.
title: When fat adapts: From physiological remodeling to disease

abstract: Cannabis is the world’s most-used illicit psychoactive plant, yet direct prehistoric evidence for its consumption is rare. In this study, we present the earliest direct evidence of cannabis use: offerings of plant parts and chemical compounds in ancient human hair recovered from a monumental tomb in Siberia. The findings suggest that the plant was used for its psychoactive qualities across Eurasia, where specific wild populations might have had naturally higher active compound levels. We show that the practice of cannabis consumption dates back at least 2800 years, anchoring debates around contemporary usage and informing discussions on cannabis in medicine, public health, law, and industry.
title: Direct evidence for psychoactive cannabis use 2800 years ago

abstract: How and when the subduction megathrust recovers its locking state after a great earthquake is important to understanding earthquake-cycle physics and future hazards. Here we report the delineation of the relocking process after the 2011 magnitude 9 Tohoku earthquake with 14 years of postseismic seafloor geodetic observations. These data, combined with onshore geodetic observations, analyses of repeating earthquakes, and numerical modeling, reveal how the recovery of locking is interrupted by afterslip on the megathrust and accompanied by stress relaxation in the viscoelastic upper mantle. The results indicate that the megathrust has already arrived at a locking state today similar to that before the earthquake despite the ongoing stress relaxation. The acquired knowledge aids understanding of megathrust earthquake cycles at other subduction zones.
title: Seafloor geodesy delineates fast megathrust relocking after the giant 2011 Tohoku earthquake

abstract: Elastocaloric cooling (eC) uses shape memory alloys (SMAs) as energy-efficient, eco-friendly refrigerants. However, cost-effectively fabricating SMAs into fatigue-resistant, heat transfer–enhanced structures remains a key obstacle to commercialization of the eC technology. We introduce a “stamping and stacking” (S-S) method for producing porous, fatigue-resistant SMA structures. Honeycomb-like chips are stamped from nitinol (NiTi) thin sheets and then stacked into a layered tubular structure to increase heat exchange surface and at the same time avoid buckling and splitting failures encountered in existing SMA structures. The stacked structure endures >10 8 compression cycles and can deliver high specific cooling power of 3850 watts per kilogram. Our S-S method reduces fabrication costs by one order of magnitude compared with existing approaches, enabling mass production of eC refrigerant structures for commercial deployment.
title: Stacked porous NiTi structure with low cost and ultrahigh fatigue life for elastocaloric cooling

abstract: Abstract A longstanding challenge in developmental science is to understand how children learn language from naturalistic everyday input. To study this process, we leveraged the First 1,000 Days (1kD) dataset, which provides longitudinal, ultra-dense daily audiovisual recordings for individual children in their home environments. This unusually detailed, child-specific record of early experience enabled us to pair each child’s rich language input with a cognitively grounded learning agent, linking naturalistic experience (“nurture”) to internal learning mechanisms (“nature”). Trained incrementally on each child’s input without prior linguistic knowledge, the learning agent discovered speech units corresponding to the English phoneme inventory and acquired thousands of words, closely mirroring individual developmental trajectories. Learning generalized across children while preserving individual differences in rate and timing. Interestingly, learning relied not only on linguistic input but also on the rehearsal of past experiences at the end of each training day. These findings demonstrate that everyday environments provide sufficient structure for language acquisition and establish a unified mechanistic framework for studying development in real-world contexts.
title: The first 1000 days: Modeling language learning from individual children’s everyday speech

abstract: Correct interpretation of evidence is essential in a rapidly evolving medical landscape
title: GLP-1 therapies and cancer risk

abstract: Obesity is now widely recognized as a chronic progressive condition. The altered biological mechanisms that cause obesity frequently require long-term treatment, including pharmacotherapies or bariatric surgery. In recent decades, the pathophysiology of obesity has been understood to an extent that obesity management medication (OMM) discovery could be rationally pursued. Advances in defining the regulation of food intake and energy expenditure by molecular communication from peripheral organs to the brain led to the development of OMMs that appear capable of safely achieving scalable and sustained body weight loss. However, side effects, heterogeneous treatment responses, long-term metabolic adaptations, adherence, and other factors may limit the use of existing OMMs and justify the development of additional medications to improve the health of people living with obesity.
title: Obesity management medications: The way forward

abstract: The 2020 United States Census adopted differential privacy to protect individual confidentiality, adding calibrated noise to summary demographic measurements that are then reconciled into population tables. We developed BlueDown, a postprocessing algorithm that combines techniques from linear regression and constrained optimization while exploiting measurement structure for efficiency. On 2020 Census data, BlueDown reduced the error of groupings by race at the county level by 21 to 36% and of all county-level groupings by 9 to 58%; at the tract level, it reduced error of groupings by housing type by 38 to 61%. These gains came at no cost to confidentiality or computational efficiency and would improve the validity of research relying on this definitive dataset and analyses used to guide the distribution of more than $1.5 trillion in annual federal spending.
title: Denoising the US Census: Succinct block hierarchical regression

title: GLP-1 receptor agonists in addiction therapy

abstract: Pharmacotherapies for obesity and type 2 diabetes are increasingly being evaluated for their effects on cognition and brain health. Evidence from preclinical models, observational cohorts, and clinical trials has intensified interest, but findings remain mixed. A central challenge is to determine whether potential cognitive effects arise from direct actions on neural circuits, indirect consequences of improved cardiometabolic health, or both. This Review examines the evidence across cardiometabolic disease, aging, and Alzheimer’s disease, focusing on glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1)–based therapies and combination approaches that engage glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, glucagon, and amylin pathways. We assess how receptor pharmacology, brain exposure, metabolic context, and disease stage shape cognitive outcomes and discuss how mechanistic clarity could guide therapies aimed at preserving or improving cognition.
title: Obesity pharmacotherapies and cognition

abstract: As the use of generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) increases, alarms are being raised about how the technology could replace human contribution, override human supervision, ignore ethical and technical guardrails, and cause increasingly irreparable harm to the environment. This creates potentially destructive outcomes for life on Earth. From a traditional Indigenous science perspective, such possibilities in themselves would be enough to immediately stop presently configured AI releases. In a Lakota context, science must ensure as little harm as possible is done to life. Therefore, AI as presently configured simply would not qualify to advance further from an ethical and scientific standpoint. Indigenous science asks something fundamentally different than what AI presently seeks to, or can, answer. But that does not mean that future forms of AI can never align with Indigenous science.
title: Can artificial intelligence align with Indigenous science?
